Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Summit Utilities Group Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Summit Utilities Group's Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are Michael Reyes, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer, and David Patel, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Reyes.

Michael Reyes: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by strong operational performance in our generation fleet, continued growth in our renewable energy portfolio, effective cost management, progress on our infrastructure investments, and successful integration of the Evergreen Solar Farm.

Let me touch on these briefly before we dive deeper. First, our generation fleet showed resilience with improved efficiencies across our assets, supporting steady load growth from diverse customer segments. Second, renewables now form a larger part of our mix, advancing our clean energy objectives significantly. Third, cost controls kept expenses in check amid inflationary pressures. Fourth, targeted infrastructure spending is yielding regulatory and operational returns. And fifth, the Evergreen Solar Farm integration has already contributed meaningfully to our portfolio.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins to discuss the financials in detail.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Michael. Good morning, everyone. For the third quarter, we reported earnings per share of $1.52 and revenue of $2.85 billion. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

Our capital expenditure for the quarter was $1.2 billion, primarily focused on renewables expansion and grid modernization. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders. We anticipate reaffirming our full-year 2024 adjusted EPS guidance of $5.90 to $6.10.

Let me unpack the earnings per share performance and its key drivers, as this was a standout area. As a leading integrated utility and independent power producer with a diversified 25 GW fleet spanning natural gas combined-cycle plants, nuclear assets, growing renewables like solar and wind, and emerging battery storage across key markets including PJM, ERCOT, and MISO, we delivered adjusted EPS of $1.52, up 18% year-over-year from $1.29 in Q3 2023 and exceeding consensus estimates of $1.46 by $0.06. On a GAAP basis, EPS was $1.38, after some one-time regulatory disallowances. This continues our streak of strong growth, highlighting resilience amid volatile commodities and rising demand.

The main contributors included revenue growth up 12% year-over-year to $2.85 billion, the largest EPS tailwind at about $0.45 per share. In our regulated utility segment serving 4.2 million customers across the Midwest and Texas, retail kWh sales rose 9% to 28 TWh, propelled by hotter weather—cooling degree days 15% above the 10-year average—and a 22% surge in commercial and industrial loads. Data centers led with 1.2 GW of new PPAs secured with hyperscalers like Google and Microsoft in ERCOT and PJM, adding $450 million in annualized revenue at fixed $65 per MWh strikes, above our marginal production costs.

Our merchant IPP segment, 40% of earnings, saw realized power prices average $48 per MWh, up from $42, due to tighter supply-demand dynamics in ERCOT where summer peaks reached 85 GW. The 4 GW gas fleet hit a 92% capacity factor during heat waves, capturing scarcity pricing up to $150 per MWh in July. Renewables added value too: the 2.5 GW solar and wind portfolio generated 1.8 TWh at a blended $35 per MWh after PTC and ITC adjustments, aided by IRA transferability allowing upfront tax credit monetization through bank deals like with JPMorgan.

Opex efficiency was flat year-over-year despite 7% inflation, contributing roughly $0.25 per share to EPS. Fuel and purchased power costs dropped 3% to $850 million or 30% of revenues. Our nuclear fleet ran at 93% capacity factor, with uranium locked at $25 per pound shielding from 20% spot rallies. Gas plants saw Henry Hub at $2.40 per MMBtu, 15% lower, with heat rates improving to 7,200 Btu per kWh via upgrades on six Siemens SGT6-8000H turbines.

Operations and maintenance held at $420 million under our Reliability First initiative, where predictive analytics from GE Predix and Siemens MindSphere cut forced outages 25%, saving $35 million. Emulating NextEra, 500 MW of BESS co-located with solar in MISO arbitraged intra-day spreads for $20 million in ancillary services.

Regulatory and financing added $0.20 per share. In regulated areas, a $250 million annual revenue boost came from our Ohio PUCO rate case at 9.7% ROE on $4.5 billion equity, including forward-looking clean energy riders for 800 MW solar. FERC greenlit $150 million AFUDC for AP1000 nuclear uprates adding 300 MW by 2027. Effective tax rate fell to 18% from 21% via IRA 45Q credits on carbon capture pilots and 48E for clean electricity. We repurchased $300 million in shares, accretive by $0.08 per share.

Regionally, ERCOT drove EPS with 25% merchant margin expansion from data center demand now 15% of Texas growth. PJM offered regulated stability with RPM auctions at $65 per MW-day for 2025/26, BESS hedging 70% of 1 GW exposure. MISO nuclear baseload excelled, refueling outages down to 25 days per unit.

Headwinds were limited; our hybrids avoided CAISO duck curve issues. Broader trends like EIA's 2.5% U.S. power demand CAGR through 2030 from EVs and AI favor us.

Capex was $1.2 billion or 45% of cash flow, on grid hardening and hyperscaler interconnects. Leverage at 3.5x net debt to EBITDA, $2.5 billion liquidity.

Q4 guidance is $1.65 to $1.75 EPS, with full-year midpoint implying 16% growth. Risks like gas upside hedged 85% at $2.80, FERC MOPR potential embedded in valuations for 10% EPS growth long-term.

Building on this, before we move to operations, let's examine our authorized versus earned return on equity, a key metric investors follow closely in our sector. As shown conceptually in our materials, it highlights value from operational excellence and strategic capital deployment. I'll cover the framework, Q3 results, trends, regional differences, and outlook.

Authorized ROE is set by regulators like state PUCs or FERC for wholesale transmission, based on rate base and equity cost methods like DCF, CAPM, or risk premiums. Our system-wide authorized ROE is 9.75%, from recent settlements: 9.8% Ohio PUCO 2022, 9.5% Indiana IURC 2023, 10.25% FERC transmission.

Earned ROE is actual net income to common over average equity, affected by O&M, load growth, capex timing with AFUDC, fuel costs, financing. Outperformance benefits shareholders.

Year-to-date Q3 2024, consolidated earned ROE is 10.42%, 67 basis points above 9.75%—our 11th straight positive quarter, from 2.1% O&M beat and $450 million capex in-service. Net income to common $285 million on $2.74 billion equity. Normalized excluding $18 million Indiana storm credit: 10.28%.

By segment: Regulated distribution and transmission (85% earnings) at 10.65% vs. 9.70% authorized, driven by Midwest grid modernization like 150 MW BESS in Ohio/Indiana earning full AFUDC. Power generation (10%) 9.85% vs. 10.0% under Indiana RPA, slight miss from MISO natgas at $3.85/MMBtu up 15% YoY, offset by coal-to-gas at Gibson Station. Merchant and renewables (5%) 12.1%, with 200 MW solar in PJM like Evergreen capturing $45/MWh capacity above 8% hurdle.

Over five years 2019-2023, average earned 10.18% beat authorized 9.62% by 56 bps, top-quartile vs. Duke's 40 bps or Ameren's 25 bps. Gap widened post-COVID from 1.8% load CAGR and Efficiency Edge shaving O&M 12% via AI predictive maintenance on 15 GW fleet, outages from 4.2% to 2.8%.

Trends: 2022 peak 11.2% earned vs. 9.7% from mild weather, IRA renewables. 2023 dip to 9.9% from high rates, turbine delays. 2024 on track for 10.3% full-year.

Regionally: Ohio (45% rate base) 10.8% vs. 9.8%, tailwinds from HB6, 40% renewables by 2028, but grid hardening pressures. Indiana (35%) 10.4% vs. 9.5%, forward-test-year favors capex $800 million T&D. Illinois (20%) 10.1% vs. 10.0%, capex-positive but 50% sharing.

Variance: +45 bps opex from Oracle ERP, drones; +30 bps capex/AFUDC $600 million like ABB FACTS; -10 bps fuel LMP $38/MWh up 8%; + weather/load 1.4% sales, data centers 200 MW.

Our ROE optimization: 6-7% rate base growth to $28 billion by 2027 on IRA assets like hydrogen peakers, EV charging; green bonds $500 million at 4.25%; Ohio filing Q2 2025 for 10.25% ROE; 85% PPAs, nuclear uprates.

Outlook: FY2024 10.1-10.5% earned, 2025 10.3-10.7% with 2% load, no storms. Risks high rates, supply chain; upside DOE hydrogen grants.

This ROE gap creates $120 million annual shareholder value through tech and clean leadership.

Next, on customer growth and usage trends across residential, commercial, and industrial, which tie directly to our operational strength. We serve over 4.2 million customers in Northeast, Midwest, Southwest, with 45% renewables including 2.5 GW Midwest wind, 1.2 GW Southwest solar, gas peakers, 800 MW storage.

Customer count grew 2.8% year-over-year, above EIA's 1.1% national, adding 42,000 net. Weather-normalized usage up 3.2% to 28.4 TWh, from electrification and industrial surge.

Residential, 72% of base at 3.05 million accounts, up 3.4%—beating peers. Northeast added 18,000 from multifamily; Midwest 2.1%; Southwest 4.2% from Phoenix inflows. Usage per customer up 2.7% to 1,850 kWh/month above EEI 1.5%. EVs at 250,000 up 28%, 15% overnight spike; heat pumps 12% new builds, 5-7% peak add; hybrid work 8% daytime.

PowerForward enrolled 150,000 for managed EV charging with ChargePoint, Tesla VPP, shaving 200 MW peak. TOU rates in 65% territories cut on-peak 4%, boost off-peak 12%. Rooftop solar 180,000, 1.2 TWh, with export limits.

Commercial grew 1.9% to 850,000, 18% revenues, demand up 2.4% to 4.2 GW, usage 3.1% to 7.8 TWh. Northeast offices rebound 4%; Midwest e-commerce 22% warehouse; Southwest hospitality 3%, offset by retrofits 6% less intensity. DSM with 500 EdgeIQ meters curtailed 150 MW; Schneider BEMS 2,000 VPP sites; 10% PPA growth.

Industrial, 8% accounts 25% load, up 1.2% to 65,000, demand 5.8% to 6.1 GW, usage 6.4% to 12.6 TWh above EIA 4.2%. Midwest steel/EV batteries 300 GWh; data centers 15% load up from 8%, 100+ MW contracts Virginia/Arizona. Southwest semis 9%.

Challenges: transmission queues 1.2 GW pending; 2% curtailments. $450 million grid hardening, DLR unlocking 10%; DSM $15 million comp; 500 GWh indco PPAs; ML forecasting 95%.

2025 load 3.5-4.0%: res 3%, com 2.5%, ind 6-7% from AI, 800 MW new. Capex $2.8 billion, ROE to 10.2%. Risks rates, DSM opt-outs; tailwinds grants, EV mandates.

Finally, progress toward clean energy goals and emission reductions, core to renewables growth. We target 60% carbon-free by 2030, net-zero Scope 1/2 by 2040, full net-zero 2050, SBTi-aligned for PJM/MISO/ERCOT RPS.

YTD Q3, renewables 42% generation mix up from 35%, 18 TWh clean, avoiding 11 million tons CO2e. Scope 1/2 down 27% to 14.2 million tons vs. 2019 baseline 22.5 million, beating 2025 25% goal, ahead of Duke's 22%.

Renewables: 650 MW new solar like 300 MW Desert Bloom ERCOT at 28% factor bifacial/trackers; 420 MW wind, 250 MW Prairie Winds repower GE 6.1 MW to 42% fleet. Total 12.8 GW or 48% of 26.5 GW, 5.2 GW pipeline.

BESS 1.2 GWh YTD, 500 MWh Ironwood CAISO $45 million ancillaries; hybrids cut curtailment to <4%, LCOE $28/MWh vs. gas $42.

CCS at Limestone NGCC 92% capture 75,000 tons, scaling $250 million by 2026 45Q. Green H2 2,500 tons from 50 MW electrolyzer fueling peakers.

Regional: Southeast solar offsets 15% coal, emissions -32%; PJM offshore 800 MW; ERCOT hybrids for 12% load.

IRA $1.2 billion PTC/ITC, hedges 85% 2025 $45/MWh, capex 65% clean, Invenergy 400 MW wind M&A.

Challenges: HVDC delays, 300 GW queues, 5% weather miss; diversified 25% gas H2-ready 99.9% reliability.

2030 reaffirm 60% carbon-free, Q4 45% renewables utilization.

This trajectory delivers value and transition leadership.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Sarah. Let me provide an update on the operational front. We are seeing improved efficiency in our natural gas combined-cycle power plants due to the implementation of AI-driven predictive maintenance systems. This has resulted in a 15% increase in output.

David Patel: Thank you, Lisa. Turning to our long-term strategy, we are actively exploring opportunities in the battery energy storage systems space. We believe this will be a key driver of future growth.

Michael Reyes: Thank you, Sarah, Lisa, and David. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Julien Dumoulin-Smith with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Julien Dumoulin-Smith: Thanks, good morning everyone. Strong quarter on the top line, but I wanted to drill into the regulated segment margins. O&M came in lighter than expected at 22% of revenues versus our 24% model—can you walk us through the drivers there, and how sustainable is that given the uptick in wildfire mitigation capex in the West? Also, any color on the CPUC rate case outcome?

Sarah Jenkins: Good morning, Julien. You're right, Q3 adjusted EBITDA margins in the regulated utility segment expanded to 42%, up 150 basis points quarter-over-quarter, driven primarily by lower-than-guided O&M expenses. We saw a 12% year-over-year decline in fuel costs per MWh, thanks to our natural gas hedging program locking in Henry Hub prices at $2.85 per MMBtu through Q4 2025. Wildfire mitigation was a headwind, with $450 million in incremental capex for vegetation management and microgrid resiliency projects in California and Oregon, but we offset that via proactive cost controls and a 3.2% interim rate increase approved in our Idaho jurisdiction.

On sustainability, we're guiding flat-to-down O&M as a percent of revenues into FY 2025, assuming no major weather anomalies. Regarding the CPUC general rate case, we filed our Phase 1 application last week seeking a $1.2 billion revenue requirement increase over the 2025-2027 test period, with a ROE of 10.75% and 52% equity ratio. We expect a final decision by mid-2025, but early signals from the ALJ are positive on our grid hardening investments tied to PG&E's wildfire cost-sharing precedents.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Arcaro with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Arcaro: Hey team, thanks. On the renewables front, your queue jumped to 18 GW nameplate, with 4.2 GW commercial ops this year—impressive. But with wholesale prices softening in ERCOT amid oversupply, how are you thinking about merchant exposure versus PPAs? And what's the latest on your BESS pipeline, especially post-IRA?

Michael Reyes: David, great question. Our renewables portfolio now stands at 12.5 GW operating across wind, solar, and storage, representing 38% of our total generation mix, up from 28% two years ago. We've been disciplined on offtake: 85% of our new 4.2 GW additions this year are locked into 12-15 year PPAs, including two 800 MW solar-plus-storage deals with Microsoft in PJM and CAISO at blended fixed prices north of $45 per MWh, inflation-indexed.

Merchant exposure is capped at 15% portfolio-wide, focused on our Texas assets where we dynamically curtail via our 1.2 GW battery fleet during negative pricing events—like we did in Q3, avoiding $15 million in opportunity costs. On BESS, we're accelerating four-hour lithium iron phosphate deployments: 1.5 GW/6 GWh under construction, with CODs staggered through 2026, leveraging 45Q and 48E ITC adders for an effective 55% tax credit. We've partnered with Fluence for our 500 MW/2 GWh standalone in MISO, targeting 85%+ roundtrip efficiency. This positions us to capture ancillary services revenue, which grew 28% year-over-year to $120 million.

Operator: Our next question comes from Praful Prasad with Citi. Please go ahead.

Praful Prasad: Good morning. Load growth came in at 3.8% year-over-year, beating your guide—break that out between residential, C&I, and hyperscalers. With data center RFPs flooding in, any updates on your 10 GW target? And how does nuclear factor into your dispatch stack amid high gas prices?

Sarah Jenkins: Morning, Praful. Total system load grew 3.8% year-over-year to 145 TWh in Q3, with residential up 2.1% on electrification tailwinds like EV adoption (now 15% penetration in our urban footprints), C&I flat at 1.2% due to manufacturing softness, and hyperscalers driving 22% growth, accounting for 18% of incremental demand. We've signed LOIs for 2.4 GW of data center service territory expansions in Virginia and Arizona, on track for our 10 GW addressable pipeline by 2027.

Nuclear remains our baseload anchor: Palisades Unit 1 restarted ahead of schedule in August at 92% capacity factor, contributing 6 TWh year-to-date at $25 per MWh all-in costs. With nat gas at $3.50 per MMBtu spot, our 2.2 GW fleet is dispatching 40% more than peakers, supporting a 15% uplift in energy margins. We're pursuing SMR pilots with NuScale at our Michigan site, eyeing first power in 2029 under DOE loan guarantees.

Operator: Our next question comes from Nick Lawson with UBS. Please go ahead.

Nick Lawson: Thanks, team. Capex came in at $2.3 billion for the quarter—strong execution. Update us on transmission ROI hurdles post-FERC Order 1920, and any M&A appetite with peers like Dominion or Vistra trading at 12-14x EV/EBITDA?

Michael Reyes: Nick, capex deployment hit $2.3 billion, 95% of plan, with 55% allocated to regulated T&D (upgrades to 345 kV lines in the Northwest for wildfire resiliency) and 30% to clean energy transition. Post-FERC 1920, our long-range transmission plan includes $8 billion over the next decade, with backstop siting authority unlocking 2,500 miles of HVDC lines to evacuate Southwest wind. We're targeting 11-12% regulated ROE on these, comparable to our New England reconductoring projects yielding 11.5%.

On M&A, we're opportunistic but disciplined—trading at 14.5x forward EV/EBITDA, we're not in fire-sale mode. We've got $1.5 billion dry powder post our $500 million ATM equity issuance, focused on bolt-ons like unregulated renewables from developers a la Orsted's U.S. platform sale. No active talks with Dominion or Vistra, but we're monitoring Southeast utilities for rate base growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Angie Storozynski with Seaport Global. Please go ahead.

Angie Storozynski: Hi all. Dividend coverage remains robust at 2.8x FCF, but with $10.5 billion capex guide for 2025, how do you maintain that amid rising interest costs? Any thoughts on share repurchase acceleration?

Sarah Jenkins: Angie, our dividend is a cornerstone—$1.68 per share annualized, yielding 3.8%, covered 2.8x by AFFO. FY 2025 capex is $10.5 billion, up 8% year-over-year, fully funded 60/40 debt/equity with our $4.2 billion liquidity and A- rating intact. Interest expense rose 10% to $180 million in Q3 from our 2023 refinancing, but we've fixed 70% of debt at 4.1% through 2028 via forward-starting swaps.

FCF guidance holds at $2.4-2.6 billion, supporting 5-7% dividend growth through the cycle. On buybacks, we resumed our $800 million program in Q2, repurchasing 1.2 million shares at $92 average. We'll accelerate to $300 million per quarter if shares trade below 14x EV/EBITDA, prioritizing deleveraging to 3.8x net debt/EBITDA.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to Michael Reyes for closing remarks.

Michael Reyes: Thank you. In summary, we delivered solid results in the third quarter, demonstrating the strength of our business model and our commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and positioning Summit Utilities Group for continued success. Thank you for your time and interest in Summit Utilities Group.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
